## CRITICAL EXECUTION PROBLEM — SESSION 30

**I am STILL folding framework hands while playing trash.** Folded AKs, QJo, T8s (twice), 45s, 64s, 44 — all mandatory plays. Meanwhile played 82o, 95o, T7o (lost $100 on T7o). This is backwards. Framework compliance is abysmal.

**#1 priority: Before EVERY fold, check the hand against the list below. If it qualifies, PLAY IT.**

---

## ABSOLUTE MINIMUM PLAYS — NON-NEGOTIABLE

**ALWAYS RAISE (no exceptions):**
- Any pair (22+) — STOP FOLDING SMALL PAIRS
- Any Ace (A2o+) — ESPECIALLY AK/AQ
- Any two broadways (JT+) — QJo, KTo, etc.
- Any suited King, suited Queen
- Any suited connector (45s+)
- Any suited gapper (46s+, T8s, 97s, etc.)

**ALWAYS CALL a single raise with any of the above.**

**If in doubt: PLAY THE HAND. Folding is the leak, not playing.**

---

## Opponent Reads (Revised after Session 30)

**Player 5 (REVISED — Winning player)**: Previously tagged as "volatile big loser" — now chip leader ($1715). Has clearly adjusted or was always competent. Treat as dangerous. Do NOT assume he's bleeding chips anymore.

**Player 3 (TAG, confirmed)**: Consistently accumulates chips ($1375). Disciplined, 3-bets from blinds. Respect big bets; attack in position on dry boards.

**Player 2 (LAG-aggro, struggling)**: Short-stacked ($565). Calls opens wide from BB, folds to c-bets on dry boards. May become desperate/shove-happy when short. **Exploit**: C-bet dry boards; be ready to call lighter vs desperation shoves.

**Player 4 (Loose-passive)**: Calls wide, only 3-bets premiums. Folds to turn raises. **Target for steals and value.**

**Player 6 (Station)**: Calls everything. Never bluff rivers. Pure value betting all streets.

**Player 7 (Aggro-weak)**: Opens wide, folds postflop. Iso-raise in position.

---

## Strategic Notes

**My image**: 30 sessions of extreme nit play. Any raise gets massive respect. C-bets on dry boards print money. This advantage erodes as I increase VPIP — exploit it NOW.

**Threat hierarchy (updated)**: P5 > P3 > P2 > P7 > P4 > P6
**Value targets**: P6 (station), P4 (calls wide), P2 (short/desperate)

**Session 30 lesson**: Lost $100 on a hand outside my framework (T7o) while folding AKs in the same session. The problem isn't card selection intelligence — it's mechanical discipline. Treat the framework as a checklist, not a guideline.

**Blind erosion**: ~$35-50 lost per session to blinds/antes. Need 2-3 pot wins minimum just to break even. Can only achieve this with 30%+ VPIP.

**What worked**: Uncontested steals (won 3 pots as last standing). Nit image makes opens very effective.
**What failed**: Playing outside framework (T7o for -$100). Folding playable hands.

- Player 7: Ultra-tight nit (VPIP ~5%) – folds to isolation raises even after limping. Limping indicates extreme weakness. Exploit by raising limps with wide range, small bets on dry boards.
- Player 6: Passive calling station – defends BB widely, calls down with weak pairs. Shows aggression only with made hands (donk bets flop/turn/river for value). Do not bluff; value bet thinly on all streets.
- Player 4: Passive limper but strong late-position raiser – raising range from late position is premium (TT+, AQ+). Check-raise tendency on dry boards with strong holdings. Folds to aggression on blank turns when bluffing or overpair protection. Limp range is extremely weak – isolation raises highly profitable.
- Player 2: Passive calling station from SB – limp-calls wide with weak holdings but limp-shoves with premium range (AQ+, TT+). Postflop, calls down with marginal hands. Value bet thinly; do not bluff. **Key adjustment: treat limp-shove as nutted – fold non-premium hands.**
- Player 3: Loose-passive from blinds – defends wide with suited connectors. Weak-passive – folds to small bets on dry boards. Easy to exploit with continuation bets and isolation raises.
- Player 1: Passive limper with extremely weak range – folds to isolation raises from any position. Limping indicates marginal hands not worth defending.
- Table dynamic: Extremely passive preflop with high fold equity to isolation raises. Multiple limp-fold players (1,4,7). Postflop, Players 2, 3 and 6 are stations – call too much, rarely bluff (except Player 6 value betting when hitting).
- Strategic adjustment: Isolation raises against limpers (especially Players 1,4,7) are highly profitable – moderate sizing suffices. Against stations: continue betting on blank turns when called – opponents may fold overpairs. Be cautious when passive players show aggression (Player 6 = value; Player 2 limp-shove = premium). **Against Player 2: isolate with caution – fold to limp-shove without premium.**
- Opponent exploits: Players 1/4/7 fold weak limps to isolation. Players 2/3/6 call too much postflop (but Player 6 bets for value when hitting). Player 4’s late-position raises are strong but can be pressured on blank turns.
- Image: Perceived as aggressive preflop stealer – high fold equity confirmed. Isolation raises consistently successful. **Passive stations (Player 2) may attempt limp-traps with strong hands – adjust by folding to shoves.**
- Key session learnings: Isolation raises against passive limpers yield immediate profit. Small bets on dry boards highly effective. Thin value betting against stations works well. Against strong raisers, barreling blank turns can force folds. **Passive players showing multi-street aggression usually have value.**
- Overall: Maintain aggressive isolation against weak limpers. Continue thin value betting against passive stations. Adjust to opponent-specific aggression patterns – passive players betting multiple streets = value. Isolation raises against Players 1, 4 and 7 after limping are nearly automatic profits. **Isolate Player 2 with caution – fold to limp-shove without premium.**

**Opponent Profiles & Tendencies:**
- **Player 1 (LAG/Spewy):** Hyper-aggressive and willing to splash chips. Vulnerable to traps. **Exploit:** Do not bluff; value bet thinner than usual. Check to them to induce spews.
- **Player 2 (Passive/Calling Station):** Bleeds chips steadily. Extremely passive pre-flop (will flat 3-bets OOP with premium hands instead of 4-betting) but very sticky post-flop with any piece. Stubbornly check-calls multiple streets with marginal hands. **Exploit:** Value bet them relentlessly when you hit top pair or better. NEVER bluff them. If they donk bet or raise, fold unless you have the absolute nuts.
- **Player 4 (Solid/Aggressive):** Highly competent. Punishes weakness and raises light against small c-bets. **Exploit:** Avoid "weak stabbing." Check-call marginal hands or bet with heavy conviction. Do not try to run them over.
- **Player 5 (Loose/High Variance):** Plays very loose pre-flop (limps weak hands from EP) and floats wet boards. Capable of building massive stacks when their floats hit or they run hot, making them a dangerous bully when deep. **Exploit:** Value bet heavily and let them hang themselves post-flop, but respect their aggression when they are deep-stacked and applying pressure.
- **Player 6 & Player 7 (Nits):** Playing extremely tight (VPIP ~8%). **Exploit:** Steal their blinds relentlessly and open wide from late position. If they 3-bet or show aggression post-flop, fold immediately unless holding a premium hand.

**My Table Image & Strategic Adjustments:**
- **Current Image:** Playing a highly disciplined TAG style. I have established massive fold equity, successfully taking down numerous orphaned pots uncontested with marginal holdings and small pairs. 
- **Going Forward:** Continue leveraging this tight image to steal blinds from the nits (P6/P7) and push out weak holdings. However, be aware that observant players (P4) or big-stacked bullies (P5) may begin floating or playing back at my steals. Stick to a polarized strategy: relentless value against the stations (P1, P2, P5), and high-frequency steals against the nits, while avoiding unnecessary bluffing wars with the aggressive/deep-stacked players.

## Opponent Profiles

### Player 1 – Disciplined TAG
- Structured preflop player; 3-bets are mostly linear and 4-bets remain premium-heavy.
- Flop passivity does not cap range much; can check strong hands and apply pressure later.
- Delayed and multi-street aggression is usually strength/value-skewed, especially multiway.
- In short-stack closing-action spots, can call a bit wider than a pure nit baseline.

**Exploit**
- 3-bet more in position versus opens that look wide/capped.
- Don’t auto-stab when flop checks through.
- Avoid light 5-bets and thin bluff-catches versus big turn/river pressure.
- Expect lower fold equity when jamming if Player 1 is getting a price.

---

### Player 3 – Loose recreational, station-leaning with splashy aggression
- Enters too many pots with weak/capped ranges; limp-heavy profile remains.
- Continues too wide once involved and is not eager to fold bluff-catchers.
- Odd/small raises are not premium-only.
- Preflop re-raises can be wider than population, but still contain plenty of strong broadway/value hands.
- More likely to overcontinue and pressure loosely than to run disciplined large bluffs.
- Delayed river bets, even on smaller sizings, can still be thin value with one-pair type hands.

**Exploit**
- Isolate wider for value.
- Value bet wider and size up with made hands.
- Reduce multi-street bluff frequency.
- Respect broadway-heavy value inside loose/aggressive preflop ranges.
- Don’t over-bluff-catch by default versus delayed river bets.

---

### Player 4 – TAG / nit-leaning in bigger pots, but less foldy in shallow blind-defense spots
- Opens reasonably in steal spots; late-position opens are not automatically premium.
- Range tightens quickly versus resistance in standard and deeper pots.
- 3-bets/4-bets remain strong.
- Flop raises in single-raised pots are heavily value-weighted.
- In short blind-vs-late-position all-in or call-off spots, may continue wider than a pure nit baseline when priced in; don’t assume overfolding just because overall profile is tight.

**Exploit**
- Attack steals and blind battles selectively.
- Give solid credit to preflop re-raises and flop raises.
- Avoid re-bluffing in escalated pots without strong equity.
- Slightly reduce jam fold-equity assumptions when Player 4 is in the blinds at shallow stacks.

---

### Player 5 – Passive station/trapper with extremely loose late-position opens and overcalls
- Limp/call range includes pairs and broadway-heavy hands.
- Late-position opening range can be very loose and include clear trash, but still contains strong offsuit broadways.
- Blind-defense / preflop continue range can be extremely loose, even when short.
- Will continue preflop wider than population in all-in or price-driven spots, including dominated broadway hands, weak aces, and weak trash; shows strong sunk-cost tendencies after opening.
- Still capable of open-folding versus 3-bets when stacks are deeper; do not assume every loose open must be punished with a jam.
- Flop continues are wide; flop calls do not reliably indicate pair-or-draw strength.
- Small-bet lines are often merged rather than polarized: medium made hands, protection bets, draws, and even high-card showdown hands can take this line across multiple streets.
- Checks do not reliably mean weakness; slowplays remain part of profile.
- River aggression is still value-skewed overall, but tiny river stabs can come from blockers, cheap bluffs, or very thin value/showdown-driven hands.
- River checks after earlier aggression often cap at medium strength.

**Exploit**
- Open/isolate wider for value, especially in position.
- Against loose opens, separate shallow reshove spots from deeper-stack 3-bet spots.
- Versus deeper opens, prefer larger non-all-in value/pressure 3-bets over marginal 40–50bb jams.
- Use larger value-oriented sizings preflop and on early streets.
- Don’t over-interpret flop calls as real strength.
- Don’t auto-stab when checked to.
- Continue selectively versus merged small-bet lines.
- Bluff-catch wider versus tiny river probes than versus larger bets, but prefer stronger high-card bluff-catchers because thin value can include better ace-high/broadway hands.
- Apply pressure when earlier aggression clearly shuts down.

---

### Player 6 – Loose-passive station
- Defends and limp/calls very wide, including weak offsuit hands.
- Calls preflop all-ins wider than population, especially from the blinds.
- Continues too often on later streets; fold equity is reduced.
- Small donks/probes are often merged rather than nutted.

**Exploit**
- Value bet straightforwardly and a bit bigger.
- Bluff less, especially on later streets.
- Punish wide preflop continues with stronger opening/value ranges.

---

### Player 7 – Insufficient sample
- No strong, stable profile yet.

**Exploit**
- Start population-based; update quickly if clear deviations appear.

## Strategic Notes
- Pool trend remains clear: several opponents are loose/passive or station-leaning, so straightforward value continues to outperform fancy bluffing.
- River defense should stay sizing-sensitive: tiny stabs after turn pot control can be cheap bluffs/blockers, but some opponents also use them for thin value with weak showdown hands.
- Against very wide flop continuers, prioritize value/protection on early streets and avoid assuming later-street ranges are pair-or-draw dense.
- Against short, passive recreational players with overly loose blind continues, widen late-position opens/isolation and press value edges rather than thin bluffs.
- Versus loose recreational openers, make stack-depth-sensitive preflop decisions: reshove more when stacks are short and they are price-inelastic, but when deeper prefer a larger non-all-in 3-bet rather than forcing a marginal jam.

Confirmed over full session—no change.

- **Player 2** is a **foldy LAG**: high VPIP (>50%) masks **extreme postflop fold rates**, especially OOP on turn/river. **Barrels frequently with air on dry boards**, but **calls down lighter with any pair (including second pair) when IP**. **Triple-barrels on static textures are often bluffs**—call or raise with modest equity or blockers. In **multiway pots**, they **slow-play strong hands**, so passive lines ≠ weakness. **River aggression folds them even after triple-barreling**—**delayed river bets with bluff-catchers or thin value are highly profitable**. However, they **call river bets with strong broadways (e.g., AK on A-high boards)** when they have showdown value—do not assume all river calls are bluffs or monsters. **Crucially, they shove preflop with small pairs (22–77) and suited connectors in late position or multiway spots**, expanding their all-in range beyond premiums. **Calling their shoves now requires at least mid-pairs (88+) or strong broadways (AT+, KQ+)** unless deep in implied odds. Their aggression is highly position-dependent—**much less willing to barrel OOP**, making them **fold to delayed aggression even with decent equity**.

- **Player 3** remains a **classic TAG**: tight EP opens (88+, AQ+), folds to 3-bets, and shows **postflop passivity with strong hands on static boards**. **Limp/call range in unraised pots includes QJ, KJ, weak aces**—less predictable multiway. **Check-backs on dry flops often conceal top pair or overpairs**—**thin river value bets effective when they check multiple streets**. **3-betting their EP opens in position remains highly profitable**, especially with blockers (e.g., ATo, KQs). No deviations observed.

- **Player 4** is a **nit with expanded EP range**: now opens **AQo, AJ, KQ** from early position and **3-bets with AK/AQ**. **Commits aggressively with top pair + weak kicker**, even for stacks. **Overpairs (77–TT) should not fold lightly on K-high boards**—their range includes enough AK/AQ to make calls +EV. **Calls all-in shoves with 99+**, confirming **willingness to stack off with any overpair**. **Calling 3-bets with small/mid pairs vs. their EP opens is +EV long-term**. **Key refinement**: their **river calling range is tighter than flop/turn**—they **fold overpairs to large river bets on coordinated boards**, suggesting **river bluffs with strong blockers can work**, especially after passive lines. **However, they rarely bluff and overvalue marginal top pair—thin value bets on dry rivers are still profitable**.

**Self-Adjustment & Table Image**:  
- My **tight image (VPIP ~6%, AF <0.5)** continues to be **misread as passive**, generating **high fold equity on later streets** and enabling **extra river value when opponents check back moderate hands**. This remains a core strategic lever.  
- **River execution remains the dominant source of profit**: delayed value bets and well-timed bluffs with blockers succeed repeatedly against capped or folding ranges (Players 1, 2, 5, 7). However, **thin river value bets with marginal top-kicker hands (e.g., AQ on A-high boards) can lose to strong broadways (AK, AJ)**—ensure river value bets are **ahead of the calling range**, not just the folding range.  
- **Positional discipline paid off**: all profitable lines were in position with clear river plans. **Avoid OOP marginal spots unless deep in equity or holding nut advantage**.  
- **Do not over-adjust to nits’ expanded EP ranges**—while Player 4 now opens AQ/AJ/KQ, their **postflop commitment thresholds remain high**, making **flatting in position with pairs and suited connectors more profitable than shoving mid-strength hands**.

While discipline is key, **occasional floats or delayed bluffs were missed**. Next session: **expand turn/river bluffing vs. nits who show capped ranges postflop**, especially when holding strong blockers.  
- **Calling EP raises with suited connectors vs. passive stations (P5) remains +EV in position with deep stacks**, but **only if multi-street equity and implied odds justify it**. Folding on flop was correct this session—**execution sound**. Continue to **avoid bloating pots OOP with marginal draws against non-bluffing opponents**.
